objectives: Reason about ocean heat content + 90% of warming.

slides.title: Ocean heat content: where the heat is
slides.body:
>90% of the **excess heat from anthropogenic greenhouse-gas forcing** accumulates in the ocean. Why: ocean has ~1100× the heat capacity of the atmosphere; large heat capacity = slow temperature response to forcing.

**Ocean heat content (OHC)**: total thermal energy stored above a reference (often 0 °C). Global ocean OHC (0-2000 m) has increased ~400 ZJ (10²¹ J) since 1955 — equivalent to ~10× current annual global energy consumption.

Distribution:
- Surface (0-100 m): warmed ~0.6 °C since 1970.
- 0-700 m: warmed ~0.3 °C since 1971.
- 700-2000 m: warmed ~0.1 °C; accelerating.
- >2000 m: warming detected but small (~0.03 °C).

Accelerating: 1971-2010 average ~0.4 W/m² globally; 2010-2020 ~0.6-0.8 W/m². Rate of OHC increase ~tripled since 1990s.

**Measurement systems**:
- Pre-2000: ship-based XBT (eXpendable BathyThermograph) profiles; limited spatial + depth coverage.
- 2000+: **Argo array** — 4000+ autonomous profiling floats; T + S 0-2000 m globally; profile every 10 days. Revolutionary; pre-Argo OHC estimates had ~30% uncertainty; now ~5%.
- Deep Argo (post-2018): extends to 6000 m. Slowly growing fleet.
- BGC-Argo: biogeochemical (O₂, NO₃, chlorophyll, pH, etc.); ~1500 floats.

Climate models use OHC as a 'gold standard' validation of forcing-response chain. Modern models match observed OHC trend to within ~10% in CMIP6.

slides.title: Sea-level rise: components + acceleration
slides.body:
Global mean sea level (GMSL) has risen ~24 cm since 1880. Rate accelerating:
- 1900-1990: ~1.5 mm/yr (linear).
- 1993-2010 (satellite altimetry era): ~3.2 mm/yr.
- 2010-2020: ~4.5 mm/yr.
- Recent: ~5+ mm/yr.

**Components**:
• **Thermal expansion** (steric): warming water expands. Currently ~40% of GMSL rise (~1.5 mm/yr).
• **Glaciers + ice caps** (excluding Greenland/Antarctica): ~22% of rise. Most of ~210 GtC/yr loss is glacier melt.
• **Greenland Ice Sheet**: ~17% of rise. Accelerating; current loss ~270 GtC/yr.
• **Antarctic Ice Sheet**: ~7% of rise. West Antarctica thinning rapidly; East Antarctic slower.
• **Land-water storage**: groundwater extraction + reservoir building offset some — net ~5% contribution.

**Projections** (IPCC AR6, 2021):
- 2100 GMSL above 1995-2014: 
  - SSP1-2.6 (low emission): 0.28-0.55 m (likely range)
  - SSP5-8.5 (high emission): 0.63-1.01 m (likely range), 0.63-1.32 m if ice-sheet instabilities included.
- 2150 GMSL: 0.5-3 m depending on scenario + ice-sheet behavior.
- Long-term commitment: even Paris-aligned emissions → 1-3 m by 2300.

**Ice sheet 'tipping' uncertainties**:
- West Antarctic marine ice sheet instability (MISI): grounding-line retreat on retrograde-sloped bedrock could be unstable.
- Greenland ice sheet: melt + dynamic loss + ice shelf collapse could accelerate.
- Antarctic + Greenland together could contribute 1-2 m sea-level rise by 2100 if instabilities trigger.
- IPCC AR6: 'low likelihood / high impact' scenarios pushed to 2 m + by 2100 in worst case.

**Regional variation**: GMSL isn't uniform. Local rates differ from global mean by ±50% due to: ocean dynamics, gravitational + rotational effects of ice-sheet mass loss (water moves away from where ice melted), vertical land motion (glacial isostatic adjustment, sediment compaction, groundwater depletion).

Notable hot-spots: NE US coast (+8-10 mm/yr), Indian Ocean, tropical Pacific. Cold-spots: SW Pacific, near Greenland (gravitational + isostatic).

slides.title: Coastal impacts + adaptation
slides.body:
Sea-level rise impacts compound with: tides, storm surge, waves, subsidence, river flooding, sediment supply. Combined hazards drive coastal risk.

**Direct impacts**:
- **Inundation**: low-lying areas (Maldives, Pacific atolls, Bangladesh deltas, NL/FL coasts) face permanent submergence. Millions to billions of people at risk.
- **Storm surge amplification**: each cm of sea-level rise extends inland flooding from a given storm. Higher base level + storm waves overtop seawalls.
- **Saltwater intrusion**: aquifers near coast contaminated by saltwater; agriculture + freshwater supply affected (Florida, Bangladesh, California Delta).
- **Erosion**: beaches + dunes retreat; cliffs collapse; sediment supply imbalanced.
- **Wetland + mangrove loss**: 'coastal squeeze' as sea rises + developed land behind blocks retreat.

**Adaptation strategies**:
• **Protect**: seawalls, dykes, storm-surge barriers (Netherlands Delta Works, UK Thames Barrier, Venice MOSE). Effective but capital-intensive + maintenance + may fail in extreme events.
• **Accommodate**: elevated structures, flood-resilient design, retreatable urban planning. Common in NL, Netherlands, parts of US.
• **Retreat**: managed relocation of communities (Isle de Jean Charles LA, Kivalina AK in process). Politically + culturally difficult; intergenerational trauma.
• **Restore**: natural infrastructure (mangroves, oyster reefs, wetlands) provides storm + erosion protection at lower cost; multi-benefit.
• **Combine**: hybrid approaches integrating gray (concrete) + green (ecosystem) + retreat over time.

**Economic costs**: trillions of USD globally for 21st century. Concentrated in coastal megacities (Shanghai, Mumbai, Lagos, Bangkok, Manila, Jakarta, NYC, Miami). Adaptation alone won't solve; combined with emission cuts is the only path.

**Equity**: SLR disproportionately impacts low-income + LMICs (Bangladesh, Pacific atoll nations, sub-Saharan Africa). Compounding with existing vulnerability. Loss-and-Damage finance (COP27 2022) addresses some — but funding far below needs.

**Long-term outlook**: SLR continues for centuries to millennia after emissions stop, due to slow thermal-expansion adjustment + ice-sheet response. Effectively irreversible on human timescales. Mitigation today determines magnitude of long-term commitment.

**Recent acceleration evidence (2020-2024)**: NASA + ESA altimetry showing further rise-rate acceleration, particularly in subtropical regions; ocean heat content rising at unprecedented rate; ice-sheet mass loss continuing. Underscores urgency.

question.question: Decompose contributions to recent sea-level rise
question.goal: Global mean sea-level rise rate is ~4.5 mm/yr (2010-2020 average). Decompose into thermal expansion, mountain glaciers, Greenland, Antarctica, land-water.

steps.reveal: Thermal expansion ~40% of total = ~1.8 mm/yr. Driven by ocean warming (heat capacity × coefficient of thermal expansion).
Mountain glaciers ~22% = ~1.0 mm/yr. Includes Alaska, Patagonia, Himalaya, Andes, Iceland, etc. Accelerating; many small glaciers projected gone by 2100.
Greenland ~17% = ~0.8 mm/yr. ~270 Gt/yr loss currently. Accelerating since 1990s.
Antarctica ~7% = ~0.3 mm/yr now; rapidly accelerating in West Antarctic. Potential for major future contribution if marine ice-sheet instability triggers.

hints: Net of groundwater depletion + reservoir storage.
steps.reveal:
Net ~0 mm/yr or slightly positive (~0.1-0.3). Groundwater extraction adds to sea level; reservoir construction holds water on land. Net effect depends on relative rates. Recent: groundwater depletion exceeding reservoir filling (now most major reservoirs built) → small net positive contribution.

**Total decomposition** (~4.5 mm/yr in 2010-2020):
- Thermal expansion: 1.8 mm/yr (40%)
- Glaciers: 1.0 mm/yr (22%)
- Greenland: 0.8 mm/yr (17%)
- Antarctica: 0.3 mm/yr (7%)
- Land water: 0.1 mm/yr (3%)
- Other / residual: 0.5 mm/yr (11%) — accounts for measurement uncertainty + glacial isostatic adjustment + small components

question.question: Order these sea-level-rise contributors by their *equilibrium / committed long-term contribution* (smallest to largest if all current warming is held).

items.label: Thermal expansion (committed to ~2-3 m for current warming)
Mountain glaciers (committed to ~0.4 m, then exhausted)
Greenland ice sheet (committed to ~7 m if fully melted)
West Antarctic Ice Sheet (committed to ~3-5 m if collapsed)
East Antarctic Ice Sheet (committed to ~50 m if fully melted)

question.explanation:
Long-term sea-level commitments (full melt of each component):
• **Mountain glaciers**: ~0.4 m total — limited mass.
• **Thermal expansion**: ~2-3 m for current warming (slow response; centuries-millennia).
• **West Antarctic Ice Sheet**: ~3-5 m if MISI triggered + the ice sheet destabilizes.
• **Greenland Ice Sheet**: ~7 m if fully melted (millennia).
• **East Antarctic Ice Sheet**: ~50 m if fully melted (but unlikely on any human timescale; mostly grounded above sea level; less marine-ice-sheet vulnerability).

These are equilibrium / 'commitment' values for current temperatures, not 21st-century projections. Greenland + WAIS each have potential tipping points where ongoing warming locks in irreversible loss over millennia. EAIS more stable on Quaternary timescales. Reaching equilibrium can take centuries-millennia; near-term projections are much smaller. But COMMITMENT — future generations have inherited — is set by today's actions.

question.question: Why does Greenland ice loss cause less sea-level rise in nearby coasts than far-away coasts (e.g., Pacific)?
options: Ice sheets have gravitational pull on surrounding water — when Greenland loses mass, the gravitational anomaly weakens + nearby water flows away. Local sea-level can DROP near Greenland by 5-10 cm per meter of equivalent sea-level rise globally. Far-field coasts (Pacific) see slightly MORE than the global average. This 'fingerprint' is so distinctive that GRACE satellite mass measurements + tide-gauge regional patterns reveal whether SLR is from Greenland vs Antarctica vs glaciers.
Greenland ice melt is mostly absorbed by nearby ground.
question.explanation:
**Sea-level fingerprints** (Mitrovica + Tamisiea 2003, key paper): each ice-sheet has a distinctive spatial pattern of sea-level change as it loses mass:

1. **Self-gravitational effect**: ice sheets gravitationally attract nearby water, holding it 'above' the geoid. When ice melts, this attraction weakens → nearby water disperses → local sea level FALLS near the source. For Greenland: within ~2000 km, sea level falls (or rises less); beyond ~6000 km, sea level rises more than the global average.

2. **Earth rotation effect**: redistributing mass changes Earth's rotation axis slightly → adjusts sea level (small but measurable).

3. **Vertical land motion (GIA)**: glacial isostatic adjustment from Pleistocene ice sheets continues; some areas (Hudson Bay, Scandinavia) still rising; offshore subsiding. Affects relative sea level on top of ice-sheet fingerprints.

**Fingerprint magnitudes (for 1 m equivalent global sea-level rise from each source)**:
- **Greenland melt**: local rise near Greenland is 0.0-0.3 m; far-field (Pacific, Indian Ocean, southern hemisphere) is 1.1-1.5 m.
- **WAIS melt**: local rise near Antarctica is 0.5-0.8 m; far-field (North Atlantic, North Pacific) is 1.1-1.2 m.
- **Glaciers + thermal expansion**: more uniform globally (smaller masses + thermal effects don't gravitationally redistribute water).

**Implications**:
- **Pacific islands** (Tuvalu, Kiribati, Marshalls) face higher SLR from Greenland melt than from local processes.
- **North America east coast**: closer to Greenland → slightly less Greenland contribution; but other processes (Gulf Stream slowdown, Atlantic OHC) add significantly.
- **Adaptation planning** uses regional projections incorporating fingerprints + dynamic effects + vertical land motion.

**Observation**: GRACE + GRACE-Follow-On satellites measure Earth's gravity field; can detect mass changes in ice sheets + their fingerprints in regional sea level patterns. Provides independent verification + tracking of ice-mass loss.

**Implication for risk**: communities far from melting ice (Pacific atoll nations, equatorial coasts) face *amplified* SLR from distant ice loss — they are paying for emissions they didn't produce, in part via this gravitational fingerprint. Equity dimension of climate change.

slides.workedSolution: Ice sheets gravitationally pull nearby water. When Greenland loses mass: attraction weakens → water disperses → local sea level falls near Greenland (within ~2000 km); rises MORE than global average in far-field (Pacific, Indian Ocean). 'Sea-level fingerprints' make ice-source attribution possible from tide gauges + altimetry. Pacific atoll nations face amplified SLR from distant Greenland melt — equity dimension. GRACE satellites confirm via gravity measurements.

question.question: Global ocean surface area is 3.6×10⁸ km² = 3.6×10¹⁴ m². If 100 Gt of ice melts, by how much does global sea level rise (in mm)? Ice mass ≈ ice volume × 917 kg/m³; melted to fresh water at 1000 kg/m³.
question.hint: 100 Gt = 10¹¹ tonnes = 10¹⁴ kg. Volume in seawater = 10¹⁴ / 1027 = 9.74×10¹⁰ m³. ÷ ocean area 3.6×10¹⁴ m² = 2.7×10⁻⁴ m = 0.27 mm.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain to a coastal city planner what '1 m of sea-level rise by 2100' actually means for planning purposes.
question.rubric: Mentions: '1 m of global mean sea-level rise' is a range (likely 0.6-1.0 m for SSP5-8.5; up to 2 m in low-likelihood/high-impact scenarios). Regional sea level may differ ±30-50% from global mean due to dynamics + ice-sheet fingerprints + vertical land motion. Local subsidence (groundwater extraction, sediment compaction) can add 1-10+ mm/yr — e.g., Jakarta sinking 25 cm/yr. Storm surge + waves + tide compound: 100-year-flood depth grows much faster than mean SLR. Inundation impacts: tens of millions globally; trillions in real estate at risk. Adaptation choices: protect (seawalls, surge barriers), accommodate (elevated buildings), retreat (managed relocation). Combined approaches typical; planning under uncertainty key. Conclude: planners should use regional + multi-scenario projections, account for compounding hazards (surge + tide + waves + subsidence), build adaptive pathways with flexible decision points, integrate with watershed + ecosystem management. Inundation is NOT just mean SLR; it's the joint hazard.
